State University, Baton Rouge We report paleomagnetic and rock magnetic data from sedimentary carbonates of the Appalachian Basin that have implications for the mechanism of widespread late Paleozoic remagnetization in this rock type. Sampling was accomplished mostly along two across-basin transects, one in Devonian carbonates of New York State and the other in Ordovician and Mississippian carbonates of Tennessee and Alabama. Paleomagnetic investigations of the New York Devonian carbonates along a transect from Albany to Buffalo indicate that these rocks were completely remagnetized in Alleghenian time. Rock magnetic studies show that magnetite concentration varies in a regular fashion along the transect with a local maximum near Syracuse and decreasing gradually to the east and west. This pattem shows a striking correlation with the degree of diagenetic alteration of clay minerals in a Devonian bentonire horizon which took place during Alleghenian time. We conclude that most of the magnetite present in these carbonates is of authigenic origin and that clay mineral alteration and magnetite authigenesis were coeval, late Paleozoic events that were controlled by the same diagenetic factors. show a very different pattern. Paleomagnetic studies indicate that late Paleozoic re- magnetization has affected Ordovician carbonates of the Nashville Dome. Paleozoic carbonates in the overthrust belt near Chattanooga also carry the late Paleozoic remagnetization. However, Mississippian carbonates between the dome and the overthrust belt are very weakly magnetized and show no evidence for late Paleozoic remagne- tization. Samples show only a present field magnetization or, at one locality in northwestern Alabama, a dual- polarity magnetization of probable Mississippian age. Rock magnetic studies indicate that higher concentrations of magnetite are present in the remagnetized rocks of the Nashville Dome and the overthrust belt than in the nonremagnetized Mississippian carbonates. We therefore conclude that magnetite authigenesis and remagnetization are related events in this setting and that the remagnetization must be due to chemical pro- cesses. However, Mississippian carbonates between the dome and the overthrust belt are very weakly magnetized and show no evidence for late Paleozoic remagne- tization. Samples show only a present field magnetization or, at one locality in northwestern Alabama, a dual- polarity magnetization of probable Mississippian age. Rock magnetic studies indicate that higher concentrations of magnetite are present in the remagnetized rocks of the Nashville Dome and the overthrust belt than in the nonremagnetized Mississippian carbonates. We therefore conclude that magnetite authigenesis and remagnetization are related events in this setting and that the remagnetization must be due to chemical pro- cesses. The presence of a remagnetization \"shadow\" in the younger rocks now exposed between the fold-thrust belt and the flexural arch is attributed to westward flow of magnetite-forming aqueous fluids through deep, sub- Carboniferous aquifers during Alleghenian time. Upward migration of the fluids through the Mississippian car- bonates may have been prevented by the Devono-Mississippian Chattanooga Shale, an impermeable stratum that is present throughout the region. These converging remagnetization circles [Halls, 1976] can be used to determine either the primary or sec- ondary magnetization direction in a two-component system, depending on which component is the least dispersed. We were able to use this method to determine the directions of remagnetizing fields that had affected our sample localities. In ideal situations, it should be possible to use converging circles in uncorrected (in situ) space to determine an over- print direction and then structurally to correct the data to produce a second set of circles and determine the primary remanence. In this nearly homoclinal section, however, structural attitudes often are too uniform to produce the necessary dispersion in one component relative to the other in order to fully utilize the method. This lack of structural variation also precluded application of the fold test to measure magnetic stability in most circumstances. We used Bingham statistics [Ohstort, 1980] to establish confidence ellipses for intersections of converging remagnetization cir- cles and conventional Fisher circular statistics [Fisher, 1953] in all other cases. These converging remagnetization circles [Halls, 1976] can be used to determine either the primary or sec- ondary magnetization direction in a two-component system, depending on which component is the least dispersed. We were able to use this method to determine the directions of remagnetizing fields that had affected our sample localities. In ideal situations, it should be possible to use converging circles in uncorrected (in situ) space to determine an over- print direction and then structurally to correct the data to produce a second set of circles and determine the primary remanence. In this nearly homoclinal section, however, structural attitudes often are too uniform to produce the necessary dispersion in one component relative to the other in order to fully utilize the method. This lack of structural variation also precluded application of the fold test to measure magnetic stability in most circumstances. pass. A total of 472 oriented cores were obtained from 39 localities shown in Figure 2. Each core was cut into two or more specimens, and the remanent magnetization of one specimen from each core was measured using a cryogenic magnetometer. Representative specimens from each locality were subjected to alternating field (af) and thermal demag- netization experiments to test the stability of remanence and to ascertain the best method of obtaining a representative magnetization direction for each particular outcrop. The af demagnetization experiments were performed using com- mercial tumbling and nontumbling specimen demagnetizers. Thermal demagnetization experiments were performed in air using a magnetically shielded oven with an internal field less than 10 gammas. Samples for chemical treatment were prepared using the multicoring method described by Henry [1979], were leached with 9 N hydrochloric acid, and were then rinsed and allowed to dry in ambient fields of less than 100 gammas. If all pilot samples from a locality had similar responses to the demagnetization experiments, one specimen from each of the remaining cores was magnetically cleaned at a peak field or temperature chosen on the basis of the behavior during stepwise demagnetization. If all pilot samples from a locality had similar responses to the demagnetization experiments, one specimen from each of the remaining cores was magnetically cleaned at a peak field or temperature chosen on the basis of the behavior during stepwise demagnetization. No single demagnetization step or procedure was appropriate for all samples at many localities, and different techniques had to be applied to individual specimens or groups of specimens. In these cases, a stable endpoint had to be determined for each specimen by analysis of directional changes during the demagnetization experiments and of the vector component diagrams of these data. The stable remanence of all specimens was then used to determine a mean direction of magnetization for each locality. These mean directions and associated statistical parameters are given in Table 1. In many instances, the principal component analysis of Kirschrink [1980] was used to analyze those sets of demagnetization vector endpoints that appeared to fall on great circle paths on an equal-area projection. Our paleomagnetic sampling of the post-Permian rocks was con- fined to the Upper Triassic Modin Formation, the Lower Jurassic Arvison Formation of Sanborn [1960], and the Lower and Middle Jurassic Potera Formation. Sanborn [1960] estimated the thicknesses of the Modin, Arvison, and Potera (with the intercalated Bagley Andesire) to be approx- imately 1680, 1550, and 520 m, respectively. We begin our presentation of results from these Permian through Jurassic strata at the lowest point in the section where a primary remanence might be expected. An unusual diorite dike that intrudes and engulfs the McCloud Lime- stone over much of the area is present also at the Nosoni Creek transect. Localities within the McCloud Limestone (Mc l, Mc2), the Nosoni Formation (No 1), and the diorite itself (mqd2, mqd3) were sampled west of the McCloud River Arm (Figure 2) in order to determine if the diorite could have remagnetized any of the strata. Paleomagnetic results from these five sites will be deferred to a later section. The declination anomalies for both Permian and Triassic strata are similar (average - 106 ø __+ 12ø), so we infer that clockwise rotation of the late Paleozoic arc did not begin until latest Triassic or earliest Jurassic time. The arc may have completed its initial rotation with respect to stable North America by Middle Jurassic time. After some retrograde motion, the arc was again facing west by the Late Jurassic, by which time some of the more westerly terranes of the province had become attached to the Eastern Klamath terrane. The composite Klamath Mountains terranes continued to rotate until the final 60 ø of clockwise rotation was nearly complete by the Early Cretaceous. Coincidence of the waning stages of rotation, at about 136 Ma, with the beginning of deposition of the basal Great Valley sequence onto the Klamath basement probably represents the completion of accretion of the Klamath Mountains terranes to the North American continent. Nearly all the rotation occurred while the Klamath Mountains terranes were part of a converging oceanic plate, with only about 20 ø of rotation in mid-Tertiary time during Basin and Range extension. METHODS USED The paleomagnetic samples were collected by use of a portable core drill and were oriented with a magnetic com- pass. A total of 472 oriented cores were obtained from 39 localities shown in Figure 2. Each core was cut into two or more specimens, and the remanent magnetization of one specimen from each core was measured using a cryogenic magnetometer. Representative specimens from each locality were subjected to alternating field (af) and thermal demag- netization experiments to test the stability of remanence and to ascertain the best method of obtaining a representative magnetization direction for each particular outcrop. The af demagnetization experiments were performed using com- mercial tumbling and nontumbling specimen demagnetizers. Thermal demagnetization experiments were performed in air using a magnetically shielded oven with an internal field less than 10 gammas. Samples for chemical treatment were prepared using the multicoring method described by Henry [1979], were leached with 9 N hydrochloric acid, and were then rinsed and allowed to dry in ambient fields of less than 100 gammas. The stratigraphic section of Permian rocks exposed along Nosoni Creek was measured and described by Coogan [1960]. There the McCloud Limestone appears to be con- formably overlain by thin interbedded gray limestone, silt- stone, tuff, and black chert assigned to the Nosoni Forma- tion. A similar sequence of rocks is seen at the contact along the west side of Lake McCloud. Although the contact seems conformable at both transects, faunal evidence [Skinner and Wilde, 1965] impl

presented abundant fossil evidence that established an age range of Late Triassic to Middle Jurassic for those units. Our paleomagnetic sampling of the post-Permian rocks was con- fined to the Upper Triassic Modin Formation, the Lower Jurassic Arvison Formation of Sanborn [1960], and the Lower and Middle Jurassic Potera Formation. Sanborn [1960] estimated the thicknesses of the Modin, Arvison, and Potera (with the intercalated Bagley Andesire) to be approx- imately 1680, 1550, and 520 m, respectively. We begin our presentation of results from these Permian through Jurassic strata at the lowest point in the section where a primary remanence might be expected. An unusual diorite dike that intrudes and engulfs the McCloud Lime- stone over much of the area is present also at the Nosoni Creek transect. Paleomagnetic results from these five sites will be deferred to a later section. Constraints on the chemical, thermal, and structural history of the Preuss are integrated with its magnetic properties to enable a close evaluation of the origin of this magnetization. The proposed origin of synfolding magnetization in the Preuss may be applicable to synfolding magnetization in other rock units. We became interested in the Preuss because it has been proposed that hydrocarbon seepage might promote growth of diagenetic magnetite and thus cause magnetic anomalies in sedimentary rock over potential hydrocarbon accumulations [Donovan et al., 1979]. Ten specimens were chemically demagnetized in an ambient field using concentrated HCl at 60øC; samples were then rinsed and dried in a reduced induction space (less than 10 nT) before measurement. Demagnetization behavior is relatively simple. One or at most two components of magnetization can be distinguished in most samples using orthogonal demagnetization diagrams [Zijderveld, 1967]. Typical demagnetization diagrams (Figure 2) show removal of a small, northerly, and steep direction with laboratory unblocking temperatures of less than 450øC. The remaining component, hereafter called the characteristic direction, is stable up to temperatures greater than 670øC. This component is observed as linear segments trending to the origin in demagnetization diagrams (Figure 2). Chemical demagnetization is very effective, partially due to high permeability, although it was not possible to apply this method to all the material collected because most samples contained calcareous cement. Both chemical and thermal demagnetization techniques isolate an identical characteristic direction in specimens of the same sample (Figures 2a and 2b). Introduction The reverse polarity Kiaman Superchron is perhaps one of the most remarkable features of the geomagnetic field in the past. For a period of about 50 m.y., including most of the Permian and part of the

ormation in Colorado [Opdyke, 1986], the lower part of which is considered to be Atokan (Middle Pennsylvanian) in age. The end of the Kiaman Superchron occurs in the Permian, where it is followed by the Illawarra mixed polarity interval of Irving and Parry [1963]. Rarely observed, normal geomagnetic polarities have been reported in Upper Permian sequences in the Soviet Union [Khramov and Rodinov, 1981], northwest Argentina [Valencio et al., 1977], southwest United States [Peterson and Nairn, 1971], and southern China [Zhao and Coe, 1987; Heller eta!., 1988]. Thus the upper boundary is placed in the Late Permian. We report dual-polarity paleomagnetic data from well-dated Upper Permian red beds from stable North America that yield a reliable Late Permian cratonic paleomagnetic pole. This result allows us to constrain the age of the end of the Kiaman interval, and improves the determination of the Late Permian segment of the North American apparent polar wander path (APWP). The paleopole deviates from the paleomagnetic Euler pole (PEP) track of Gordon eta!. [1984], suggesting that North American plate motion was not constant relative to the rotation axis throughout the Late Carboniferous-Early Triassic interval, as has previously been argued [Gordon et al., 1984]

CALDERONE U.S. Geological Survey, Flagstaff, Arizona ROBERT F. BUTLER AND GARY D. ACTON 1 Department of Geosciences, University of Arizona, Tucson Paleomagnetic directions have been obtained from 190 early to middle Miocene (12-20 Ma) mafic volcanic flows in 16 mountain ranges in the Mojave-Sonora desert region of western Arizona and southeastern California. These flows generally postdate early Miocene tectonic deformation accom- modated by low-angle normal faults but predate high-angle normal faulting in the region. After detailed demagnetization experiments, 179 flows yielded characteristic directions interpreted as original thermal remanent magnetizations (TRM). Because of the episodic nature of basaltic volcanism in this region, the 179 flows yielded only 65 time-distinct virtual geomagnetic poles (VGPs). The angular dispersion of the 65 VGPs is consistent with the angular dispersion expected for a data set that has adequately averaged geomagnetic secular variation. The paleomagnetic pole calculated from the 65 cooling unit VGPs is located at 85.5øN

Assuming that the maximum temperature of 200OC lasted for a period of 2x108 years, then laboratory blocking temperatures of about 450OC would be expected [Middleton and Schmidt, 1982], which is 60o lower than the blocking temperatures we observed in the laboratory (510oC). This would suggest that the magnetization observed in the thrust sheets is unlikely to have been of thermo-viscous origin. However, Kent [1985] has argued that there is a large degree of uncertainty about the time/temperature relationship for thermoviscous remagnetization of magnetites in limestones. Thus thermoviscous magnetization cannot be entirely ruled out for the origin of the observed synfolding remagne- tizations. The speleothems, which are composed of light and dark calcite bands, occur in caves of karst origin in the Ordovician Kindblade Formation. Vertebrate fossils interbedded with the deposits indicate they are Permian in age. The dark bands contain primary hydrocarbon-filled fluid inclusions. The presence of authigenic magnetite spheres in magnetic extracts of the dark calcites supports a chemical origin for the magnetization. Shallow burial depths probably eliminate the possibility of a thermoviscous magnetization. The

Although the results from Cement are controversial, recent studies have demonstrated that there is a relationship between hydrocarbons and authigenic magnetite. For example, Elmore et al. [1987] and McCabe et al. [1987] report the presence of authigenic magnetite in samples of solid bitumen that is biodegraded. Elmore et al. JOURNAL OF GEOPHYSICAL RESEARCH, VOL. 95, NO. B4, PAGES 4539-4549, APRIL 10, 1990 REMANENCE IN AUTHIGENIC MAGNETITE: TESTING THE HYDROCARBON-MAGNETITE HYPOTHESIS R. Douglas Elmore and Lisa Crawford School of Geology and Geophysics, University of Oklahoma, Norman Abstract. Paleomagnetic, rock magnetic, petrographic, and geochemical studies of hydrocarbon-saturated speleothems in southern Oklahoma indicate there is a relation between hydrocarbons and a chemical magnetization that resides in magnetite. The speleothems, which are composed of light and dark calcite bands, occur in caves of karst origin in the Ordovician Kindblade Formation. Vertebrate fossils interbedded with the deposits indicate they are Permian in age. The dark bands contain primary hydrocarbon-filled fluid inclusions. The dark calcites possess over an order of magnitude stronger natural remanent magnetization than the lighter bands which do not yield stable decay during demagnetization. Alternating field (AF) and thermal demagnetization of specimens of the dark bands reveal a Permian direction of magnetization (declination=160, inclination=3, k=17, 95=5, n=56). The results of rock magnetic experiments, and the fact that most maximum unblocking temperatures are below 580øC, suggest that the d

e of authigenic magnetite spheres in magnetic extracts of the dark calcites supports a chemical origin for the magnetization. Shallow burial depths probably eliminate the possibility of a thermoviscous magnetization. The occurrence of primary hydrocarbon inclusions suggests that hydrocarbons seeped into the caves during precipitation of the speleothems and were trapped in the calcite crystals. The relationship between intensity of magnetization and hydrocarbon abundance leads us to propose that chemical conditions created by the hydrocarbons caused precipitation of authigenic magnetite and acquisition of the associated chemical remanence. Introduction Secondary magnetizations that reside in magnetite and were acquired long after deposition have been reported from several units [e.g., Benthien and Elmore, 1987; McCabe et al., 1983, 1984; Wisniowiecki et al., 1983]. Authigenic magnetite has been reported from these units, and the magnetizations are interpreted as chemical (i.e., diagenetic) in origin. A chemical origin for these magnetizations, however, is controversial from several viewpoints. For example, as demonstrated by Kent [1985], a thermoviscous origin caused by moderately elevated burial temperatures is also a permissible interpretation for some second

sted that the magnetite reported by Donovan et al. [1979] represents contamination from drilling, but did report ferrimagnetic pyrrhotite and suggested that it precipitated as a result of hydrocarbon-related fluids. Although the results from Cement are controversial, recent studies have demonstrated that there is a relationship between hydrocarbons and authigenic magnetite. For example, Elmore et al. [1987] and McCabe et al. [1987] report the presence of authigenic magnetite in samples of solid bitumen that is biodegraded. Elmore et al. [1987] also present preliminary evidence that hydrocarbons can cause acquisition of a stable remanence in authigenic magnetite. In this paper the detailed evidence for a genetic relationship between hydrocarbons and acquisition of a chemical remanence is presented. The principal evidence for a genetic relationship between hydrocarbons and acquisition of a chemical remanent magnetization (CRM) comes from the study of hydrocarbon-bearing, late Paleozoic speleothems which are found in caves of karst origin in the Lower Ordovician Arbuckle Group in southern Oklahoma. Analysis of Paleomagnetic Data The characteristic remanence directions derived from the progressive demagnetization data were averaged by cooling unit in order to determine the mean direction and statistical error limits of the various units (Table 2). These flow means were then used to evaluate the stability of the paleomagnetic directions, so as to guard against interpreting overprinted directions as primary directions. The stability tests applied to this data set consisted of a penecontemporaneous intrusion test and a fold test. The intrusion test is a simple comparison of mean remanence directions obtained from flows and from dikes intruding the flows. After progressive thermal demagnetization of all samples at six steps from 350øC to 630øC, 89 samples were selected for final paleopole analysis on the basis of their magnetic stability. These results indicate that no discernible rotation or displacement of the Maya block has occurred since at least early Neocomian times. PALEOMAGNETIC RESULTS Our experimental plan was originally designed with the intention of expanding the Opdyk£ and Wensink [1966] study by comprehensive sampling of Jurassic plutons in New England. We soon realized that progressive alternating field (AF) and thermal demagnetizations on the initial collection of plutonic rocks simply confirmed the existence of a single component, normal polarity magnetization. However, a pilot study on the Moat volcanics revealed more complex, multicomponent magnetizations and we thus concentrated on this more promising rock unit. All magnetization components identified from progressive demagnetization were analyzed with principal component analysis [Kirschvink, 1980] and mean directions calculated according to standard Fisher [1953] statistics. Field evidence suggests that the Tarim Block collided with the Tian Shah arc in Carboniferous to Permian times [Wang and Liu, 1981; ghang et al., 1984; Chen and Liang, 1985; 7_2ang and Wu, 1985; Watson et al., 1987; Hu, 1985; Smith, 1988; Gao and Wu, 1984; Ji and Coney, 1985]. Because the Tarira Block is the most inboard block of China, an understanding of its motion is important in constructing the history of terrane accretion to the south. Permian, Carboniferous and Devonian palcomagnetic poles for Tarim were reported by Bai eta/. [ 1987], but none of these results were substantiated by field tests such as fold, contact or conglomerate tests. A reliable apparent polar wander path for a block as large as Tarira requires paleomagnetic results from many widely distributed sections, and thus we began a coml:rrehensive paleomagneiic sampling program in Tarira to measure the displacement of Tarira with respect to the Siberian, North China and South China Blocks (Figure 1). During the summer of 1986, a palcomagnetic study of the Tarira Block was undertaken jointly by members of the Xinjiang Geology Research Institute, the Beijing Graduate School of China University of Geosciences, Chinese Academy of Geological Sciences and the Geophysics Department at Stanford University. s to Permian times [Wang and Liu, 1981; ghang et al., 1984; Chen and Liang, 1985; 7_2ang and Wu, 1985; Watson et al., 1987; Hu, 1985; Smith, 1988; Gao and Wu, 1984; Ji and Coney, 1985]. This is a likely time for intrusion of the normal polarity lamprophyre dikes and the Nemegosenda carbonatite, the closest large Keweenawan complex to the C component sites. Evidence for both minor later faulting and localized hydrothermal effects is seen in minor fault offsets found in the 1.1 Ga Lacknet Lake and Nemegosenda carbonatite complexes [Parsons, 1961], and in the 1.8 to 1.7 Ga and 1.2 to 1.0 Ga K/At and 40Ar/39Ar age dates found near the ILCZ [Archibald et al., 1986; Lopez Martinez and York, 1986]. The latter direction corresponds to an age of about 1085 Ma on the APWP in the midst of the long normal superchron of Halls and Pesonen [1982]. This is a likely time for intrusion of the normal polarity lamprophyre dikes and the Nemegosenda carbonatite, the closest large Keweenawan complex to the C component sites. Thus the C component could be a localized hybrid of the B component and a Keweenawan normal chemical remanent magnetization (CRM), both residing in similar high coercivity and unblocking temperature spectra. Alternatively the C component could be a tilted B component because the correction of C for a 40 ø WNW tilt aligns it almost perfectly with B. This alternative requires minor local- ized block faulting along subsidiaries of the ILCZ after 1.88 Ga. Evidence for both minor later faulting and localized hydrothermal effects is seen in minor fault offsets found in the 1.1 Ga Lacknet Lake and Nemegosenda carbonatite complexes [Parsons, 1961], and in the 1.8 to 1.7 Ga and 1.2 to 1.0 Ga K/At and 40Ar/39Ar age dates found near the ILCZ [Archibald et al., 1986; Lopez Martinez and York, 1986]. The latter direction corresponds to an age of about 1085 Ma on the APWP in the midst of the long normal superchron of Halls and Pesonen [1982]. This is a likely time for intrusion of the normal polarity lamprophyre dikes and the Nemegosenda carbonatite, the closest large Keweenawan complex to the C component sites. Thus the C component could be a localized hybrid of the B component and a Keweenawan normal chemical remanent magnetization (CRM), both residing in similar high coercivity and unblocking temperature spectra. Alternatively the C component could be a tilted B component because the correction of C for a 40 ø WNW tilt aligns it almost perfectly with B. This alternative requires minor local- ized block faulting along subsidiaries of the ILCZ after 1.88 Ga. Evidence for both minor later faulting and localized hydrothermal effects is seen in minor fault offsets found in the 1.1 Ga Lacknet Lake and Nemegosenda carbonatite complexes [Parsons, 1961], and in the 1.8 to 1.7 Ga and 1.2 to 1.0 Ga K/At and 40Ar/39Ar age dates found near the ILCZ [Archibald et al., 1986; Lopez Martinez and York, 1986]. carrier_investigation_candidates.excerpt: J. THORKELSON Department of Earth Sciences, Carleton University, Ottawa-Carteton Geoscience Centre, Ottawa, Canada The Spences Bridge Group of late Albian age (palynology and U/Pb zircon date of 104.5 Ms) is situated in the Intermontane Belt of the southern Canadian Cordillera. Zeolite-grade andesire lavas and interbedded volcaniclastic rocks have been sampled through a thickness of about 2900 m. Sampling has been confined to localities whose bedding attitudes are well defined and to rocks that have not undergone internal deformation. Of the 27 sites studied, 25 gave single-component magnetizations with well-grouped directions, high coercivities and high unblocking temperatures. Applying corrections for geological tilt to all 25 sites yielded minimum dispersion after 65% untilting. Analysis indicates that this is a consequence of the interaction of two modes of behavior, one (exhibited by Y magnetizations at 8 sites) in which minimum dispersion occurs after 35% untilting, and one (X magnetizations at 17 sites) in which minimum dispersion occurs after 100% correction. (Actually the dispersion is essentially constant in the range 88 to 100% correction). The Y magnetizations are uninterpretable in terms of the paleofield because no estimate of paleohorizontal can be made. B

carrier_investigation_candidates.excerpt: Marquis and Globerman [1988] have estimated 1500 +_ 950 km of northward movement from the paleomagnetism of bedded volcanic rocks of the Carmacks Group (70 Ma) of the northern Intermontane Belt (CK of Figure 1). Their data pass the tilt test, so that syntilting and posttilting magnetizations are either absent or neglible. One weakness in their argument, which they acknowledged, was that the cratonic reference field for the latest Cretaceous is less secure than that for mid-Cretaceous time. This weakness has to some extent been lessened by the recent publication of new cratonic data as will be described below [Swenson and McWilliams, 1989]. The Carmacks Group is 30 Ma younger than plutons from which the discordances of Figure 1 have been observed. The data we are about to describe are from a 2900- m sequence of bedded mid-Cretaceous rocks, the Spences Bridge Group, that are essentially coeval with these plutons. The rocks are located in the southern part of the lntermontane Belt (SB of Figure 1). TECTONIC SETTING Traditionally, the Canadian Cordillera has been divided into five morphogeologic belts arranged in a generally NW-SE configuration. These belts are distinguished on the basis of their geology and physiography, and have complex geological histories

In hand specimen the andesites are gray with a bluish or reddish tinge. During drilling the mud produced varies from gray to reddish brown. Finely disseminated hematite is a common constituent. Primary volcanic textures are preserved, and there is no evidence of secondary petrofabrics [Devlin, 1981; Thorkelson, 1986]. Metamorphic grades are within the zeolite facies [Devlin, 1981]. None of the flows sampled show evidence, in either thin section or in outcrop, of internal deformation. In places slickensides are associated with some faults, but such outcrops have been deliberately avoided. Clastic deposits, which constitute about half of the formation, include air- fall and ash-flow tuff, lahar, conglomerate, sandstone and shale. Calc-alkaline major and trace element characteristics suggest a subduction- generated origin [Thorkelson, 1985, 1987; Smith, 1986; Thorkelson and Smith, 1989]. The overlying Spius Formation is geographically located in the center of the main Spences Bridge Group outcrop, but correlative rocks may occur in the northwestern outlier (Figure 2, K. G

east of the sampling locality. In the Intermontane Belt, apparent displacements calculated from paleomagnetic data from the Carmacks Group, and from the Spences Bridge X data are in agreement with one another (SBI and CK1 of Figures 18 and 19). As already noted, the former study, like that herein, includes a positive tilt test, but unlike that herein suffers from uncertainty in the cratonic reference paleopole for Late Cretaceous time [Marquis and Globerman, 1988]. Very recently, new data from the Maudlow Formation of Montana (83 to 75 Ma) have provided further information on the reference field for this time [Swenson and McWilliams, 1989]. The revised reference paleopole calculated from the three cratonic paleopoles listed by Marquis and Globerman [1988] and the above is 76.9øN, 197.1'E (N -- 4, K -- 0205, Aos = 6.4). The four rock units from which these paleopoles were derived span the interval 83 to 63 Ma embracing the time when the Carmacks Group was deposited (70 Ma). Entry CK2 of Table 4 has been calculated from the result of Marquis and Globerman [1988] and the above cratonic reference paleopole. Entry CK3 has been calculated using the reanalysis of the Carmacks Group data by Butler [ 1990] who contended that there is some redundancy in them, which h

ncordant data have now been obtained from Eocene rocks which range in age from 55 to 48 Ma and which are spread from Vancouver Island in the west to Wyoming and Montana on the craton [Beck et al., 1982; Diehl eta!., 1983; Shire and Pruss, 1977; Fox and Beck, 1985; Symons and Welling, 1989; Bardoux and Irving, 1989; Vandall and Palmer, 1990; Irving and Brandon, 1990]. Thus the younger limit to these displacements is set by the palcomagnetic data at about 50 Ma. The older limit is set by the ages of aberrant magnetizations. These are best determined for the Spuzzum pluton and for the Spences Bridge Group. In the Spuzzum pluton the blocking temperatures are 550' to 675'C so that the magnetization acquisition age very likely lies between the K-Ar ages which range 90-103 Ma in the center and west of the body, and the U-Pb zircon age of 110 Ma [Irving et al., 1985, p. 580]. For reasons given above we argue that the acquisition time of the X magnetization of the Spences Bridge Group is at or soon after deposition in the mid-Cretaceous. Present evidence therefore indicates that the apparent displacements of Figures 18 and 19 occurred sometime in the interval Late Cretaceous through Paleocene. Introduction In certain circumstances the palaeomagnetic method can be employed to date episodes of igneous intrusion where reliable age data cannot otherwise be obtained by conventional radiometric methods. It involves isolating primary directions of magnetisation from the rock body, determining the corresponding palaeomagnetic pole, and comparing this pole with the apparent polar wander (a.p.w.) path for the region independently established from studies on dated rocks. The palaeomagnetic method of dating has the advantage that many more rock units can be surveyed than is practicable with the Rb-Sr method, and it does not suffer from the difficulties of interpretation caused by variable argon loss in the K-Ar method. However, a success- ful application depends critically on a number of factors. Firstly, the age of the rock unit must be known within broad limits; secondly the

mprophyre suites also might be evaluated. 3. Palaeomagnetic results 3a. Method Samples were drilled in the field using a portable motorised drill and oriented while still attached to the outcrop by sights on the sun or by magnetic bearings in conjunc- tion with topographic sightings. A 2.5 cm long cylinder was cut from the base of each core and measured before and after progressive demagnetisation in alternating fields; the demagnetising treatment was normally continued in steps of 50 or 100 Oersteds (oe.) for all samples until either no further significant change in direction was observed or until the treatment began to introduce unstable components of magnetisation. All measurements were made with a parastatic magnetometer except those from six sites (16 to 21) in dykes intruding the Eycott Group, which were measured with a PAR SM-2D spinner magnetometer. Brown and W. A. Morris This study employs palaeomagnetism to differentiate between Palaeozoic minor intrusionsinnorthern England. The lamprophyres of the Cross Fell Inlier subdivide petrographically into kersantites and minettes. All the kersantites have steep directions of magnetisation probably correlating with an interval of anomalous geomagnetic field in Caradocian times. The Threlkeld-St John’s micro- granodiorite (445 m.y.) and Carrock Fell dolerite dyke swarm also possess steep magnetisations assigned to the same interval. The minettes have shallow directions of magnetisation similar to the Shap Granite (393 m.y.) and correlate with the later Caledonian intrusions of northern England. These episodes of intrusion are separated by late-Silurian tectonism and definea trend of increasing K20/Nar0 in the later magmas of the Caledonian orogeny. Miscellaneous palaeomagnetic results from the Borrowdale Volcanic Group, Embleton diorites and Haweswater dolerite are also reported. 1. Introduction In certain circumstances the palaeomagnetic method can be employed to date episodes of igneous in

part of the Caledonian cycle. 2. Geological outline 2a. Lake District igneous rocks Deposition of the rocks now comprising the Skiddaw Slate Group of northern England was succeeded by a whole range of intrusive and extrusive igneous rocks which may, in part, be genetically related to intrusion of the Caledonian batholith underlying the Lake District Dome and defined by gravity study (Bott 1974). The research of recent years has, however, shown that these igneous episodes occurred at several different periods between and after Caledonian tectonic events. For example, eruption of the Eycott Group of the north Lake District comprising basalts and basaltic andesites (Eastwood et al. 1965) commenced during the Didymograptus bifidus time zone of the Llanvirn (Downie and Soper 1972), and was tilted prior to eruption of the Borrowdale Volcanic Group (palaeomagnetic sites 1 to 4 of this study), comprising predominantly andesites and rhyolites (Firman 1957; Mitchell 1956; Moseley 1960, 1964). This latter group lies unconformably on Llanvirnian slates east of Keswick but may be essentially conformable in the southwest of the Lake District outcrop; it was in turn folded and partly eroded prior to deposition of the (Caradocian) Coniston Limestone Group including minor volcanic com

of the north Lake District comprising basalts and basaltic andesites (Eastwood et al. 1965) commenced during the Didymograptus bifidus time zone of the Llanvirn (Downie and Soper 1972), and was tilted prior to eruption of the Borrowdale Volcanic Group (palaeomagnetic sites 1 to 4 of this study), comprising predominantly andesites and rhyolites (Firman 1957; Mitchell 1956; Moseley 1960, 1964). This latter group lies unconformably on Llanvirnian slates east of Keswick but may be essentially conformable in the southwest of the Lake District outcrop; it was in turn folded and partly eroded prior to deposition of the (Caradocian) Coniston Limestone Group including minor volcanic components (Eastwood 1953). The Haweswater dolerite (Fig. 1 and palaeomagnetic sites 5-7 of this study) intrudes the Borrowdale Volcanic Group on either side of Haweswater and was interpreted as a vent related to the group by Nutt (1968). A 2.5 cm long cylinder was cut from the base of each core and measured before and after progressive demagnetisation in alternating fields; the demagnetising treatment was normally continued in steps of 50 or 100 Oersteds (oe.) for all samples until either no further significant change in direction was observed or until the treatment began to introduce unstable components of magnetisation. Brown and W. A. Morris This study employs palaeomagnetism to differentiate between Palaeozoic minor intrusionsinnorthern England. The lamprophyres of the Cross Fell Inlier subdivide petrographically into kersantites and minettes. All the kersantites have steep directions of magnetisation probably correlating with an interval of anomalous geomagnetic field in Caradocian times. The Threlkeld-St John’s micro- granodiorite (445 m.y.) and Carrock Fell dolerite dyke swarm also possess steep magnetisations assigned to the same interval. The minettes have shallow directions of magnetisation similar to the Shap Granite (393 m.y.) and correlate with the later Caledonian intrusions of northern England. These episodes of intrusion are separated by late-Silurian tectonism and definea trend of increasing K20/Nar0 in the later magmas of the Caledonian orogeny. Miscellaneous palaeomagnetic results from the Borrowdale Volcanic Group, Embleton diorites and Haweswater dolerite are also reported. 1. Introduction In certain circumstances the palaeomagnetic method can be employed to date episodes of igneous in

part of the Caledonian cycle. 2. Geological outline 2a. Lake District igneous rocks Deposition of the rocks now comprising the Skiddaw Slate Group of northern England was succeeded by a whole range of intrusive and extrusive igneous rocks which may, in part, be genetically related to intrusion of the Caledonian batholith underlying the Lake District Dome and defined by gravity study (Bott 1974). The research of recent years has, however, shown that these igneous episodes occurred at several different periods between and after Caledonian tectonic events. For example, eruption of the Eycott Group of the north Lake District comprising basalts and basaltic andesites (Eastwood et al. 1965) commenced during the Didymograptus bifidus time zone of the Llanvirn (Downie and Soper 1972), and was tilted prior to eruption of the Borrowdale Volcanic Group (palaeomagnetic sites 1 to 4 of this study), comprising predominantly andesites and rhyolites (Firman 1957; Mitchell 1956; Moseley 1960, 1964). This latter group lies unconformably on Llanvirnian slates east of Keswick but may be essentially conformable in the southwest of the Lake District outcrop; it was in turn folded and partly eroded prior to deposition of the (Caradocian) Coniston Limestone Group including minor volcanic com

Introduction In certain circumstances the palaeomagnetic method can be employed to date episodes of igneous intrusion where reliable age data cannot otherwise be obtained by conventional radiometric methods. It involves isolating primary directions of magnetisation from the rock body, determining the corresponding palaeomagnetic pole, and comparing this pole with the apparent polar wander (a.p.w.) path for the region independently established from studies on dated rocks. The palaeomagnetic method of dating has the advantage that many more rock units can be surveyed than is practicable with the Rb-Sr method, and it does not suffer from the difficulties of interpretation caused by variable argon loss in the K-Ar method. However, a success- ful application depends critically on a number of factors. Firstly, the age of the rock unit must be known within broad limits; secondly the

advantage that many more rock units can be surveyed than is practicable with the Rb-Sr method, and it does not suffer from the difficulties of interpretation caused by variable argon loss in the K-Ar method. However, a success- ful application depends critically on a number of factors. Firstly, the age of the rock unit must be known within broad limits; secondly the a.p.w. path must be well defined between these limits, and thirdly, a.p.w. movements should be both relatively rapid and occur frequently for the method to be of much use. The difficulties of applying palaeomagnetism to dating rocks are acute in Precambrian times when the palaeopole is known to have undergone excursions and returned to similar positions, sometimes within periods of 100 m.y., while at other times it remained essentially stationary for periods of tens of millions of years. The a.p.w. path for Britain in Lower Palaeozoic times is now sufficiently well understood for it to be considered as a practical dating tool for this interval (Briden Geol. J. Vol. 13, Pt 1,1978 73 74 J. D. A. PIPER ET AL. et al. 1973; Faller et al. 1976; Piper 1978). Brown and W. A. Morris This study employs palaeomagnetism to differentiate between Palaeozoic minor intrusionsinnorthern England. The lamprophyres of the Cross Fell Inlier subdivide petrographically into kersantites and minettes. All the kersantites have steep directions of magnetisation probably correlating with an interval of anomalous geomagnetic field in Caradocian times. The Threlkeld-St John’s micro- granodiorite (445 m.y.) and Carrock Fell dolerite dyke swarm also possess steep magnetisations assigned to the same interval. The minettes have shallow directions of magnetisation similar to the Shap Granite (393 m.y.) and correlate with the later Caledonian intrusions of northern England. These episodes of intrusion are separated by late-Silurian tectonism and definea trend of increasing K20/Nar0 in the later magmas of the Caledonian orogeny. Miscellaneous palaeomagnetic results from the Borrowdale Volcanic Group, Embleton diorites and Haweswater dolerite are also reported. 1. Introduction In certain circumstances the palaeomagnetic method can be employed to date episodes of igneous in

ntrusion of the Caledonian batholith underlying the Lake District Dome and defined by gravity study (Bott 1974). The research of recent years has, however, shown that these igneous episodes occurred at several different periods between and after Caledonian tectonic events. For example, eruption of the Eycott Group of the north Lake District comprising basalts and basaltic andesites (Eastwood et al. 1965) commenced during the Didymograptus bifidus time zone of the Llanvirn (Downie and Soper 1972), and was tilted prior to eruption of the Borrowdale Volcanic Group (palaeomagnetic sites 1 to 4 of this study), comprising predominantly andesites and rhyolites (Firman 1957; Mitchell 1956; Moseley 1960, 1964). This latter group lies unconformably on Llanvirnian slates east of Keswick but may be essentially conformable in the southwest of the Lake District outcrop; it was in turn folded and partly eroded prior to deposition of the (Caradocian) Coniston Limestone Group including minor volcanic components (Eastwood 1953). The Haweswater dolerite (Fig. 1 and palaeomagnetic sites 5-7 of this study) intrudes the Borrowdale Volcanic Group on either side of Haweswater and was interpreted as a vent related to the group by Nutt (1968). Further to the north theThrelkeld- St John's micro

section_candidates.excerpt: Palaeomagnetism and chronology of Caledonian igneous episodes in the Cross Fell lnlier and northern Lake District J. D. A. Piper, A. S. McCook, K. P. Watkins, G. C. Brown and W. A. Morris This study employs palaeomagnetism to differentiate between Palaeozoic minor intrusionsinnorthern England. The lamprophyres of the Cross Fell Inlier subdivide petrographically into kersantites and minettes. All the kersantites have steep directions of magnetisation probably correlating with an interval of anomalous geomagnetic field in Caradocian times. The Threlkeld-St John’s micro- granodiorite (445 m.y.) and Carrock Fell dolerite dyke swarm also possess steep magnetisations assigned to the same interval. The minettes have shallow directions of magnetisation similar to the Shap Granite (393 m.y.) and correlate with the later Caledonian intrusions of northern England. These episodes of intrusion are separated by late-Silurian tectonism and definea trend of increasing K20/Nar0 in the later magmas of the Caledonian orogeny. Miscellaneous palaeomagnetic results from the Borrowdale Volcanic Group, Embleton diorites and Haweswater dolerite are also reported. 1. Introduction In certain circumstances the palaeomagnetic method can be employed to date episodes of igneous in

cle. 2. Geological outline 2a. Lake District igneous rocks Deposition of the rocks now comprising the Skiddaw Slate Group of northern England was succeeded by a whole range of intrusive and extrusive igneous rocks which may, in part, be genetically related to intrusion of the Caledonian batholith underlying the Lake District Dome and defined by gravity study (Bott 1974). The research of recent years has, however, shown that these igneous episodes occurred at several different periods between and after Caledonian tectonic events. For example, eruption of the Eycott Group of the north Lake District comprising basalts and basaltic andesites (Eastwood et al. 1965) commenced during the Didymograptus bifidus time zone of the Llanvirn (Downie and Soper 1972), and was tilted prior to eruption of the Borrowdale Volcanic Group (palaeomagnetic sites 1 to 4 of this study), comprising predominantly andesites and rhyolites (Firman 1957; Mitchell 1956; Moseley 1960, 1964). This latter group lies unconformably on Llanvirnian slates east of Keswick but may be essentially conformable in the southwest of the Lake District outcrop; it was in turn folded and partly eroded prior to deposition of the (Caradocian) Coniston Limestone Group including minor volcanic components (Eastwood 1953).

The palaeomagnetic method of dating has the advantage that many more rock units can be surveyed than is practicable with the Rb-Sr method, and it does not suffer from the difficulties of interpretation caused by variable argon loss in the K-Ar method. Brown and W. A. Morris This study employs palaeomagnetism to differentiate between Palaeozoic minor intrusionsinnorthern England. The lamprophyres of the Cross Fell Inlier subdivide petrographically into kersantites and minettes. All the kersantites have steep directions of magnetisation probably correlating with an interval of anomalous geomagnetic field in Caradocian times. The Threlkeld-St John’s micro- granodiorite (445 m.y.) and Carrock Fell dolerite dyke swarm also possess steep magnetisations assigned to the same interval. The minettes have shallow directions of magnetisation similar to the Shap Granite (393 m.y.) and correlate with the later Caledonian intrusions of northern England. These episodes of intrusion are separated by late-Silurian tectonism and definea trend of increasing K20/Nar0 in the later magmas of the Caledonian orogeny. Miscellaneous palaeomagnetic results from the Borrowdale Volcanic Group, Embleton diorites and Haweswater dolerite are also reported. 1. Introduction In certain circumstances the palaeomagnetic method can be employed to date episodes of igneous in

of the north Lake District comprising basalts and basaltic andesites (Eastwood et al. 1965) commenced during the Didymograptus bifidus time zone of the Llanvirn (Downie and Soper 1972), and was tilted prior to eruption of the Borrowdale Volcanic Group (palaeomagnetic sites 1 to 4 of this study), comprising predominantly andesites and rhyolites (Firman 1957; Mitchell 1956; Moseley 1960, 1964). This latter group lies unconformably on Llanvirnian slates east of Keswick but may be essentially conformable in the southwest of the Lake District outcrop; it was in turn folded and partly eroded prior to deposition of the (Caradocian) Coniston Limestone Group including minor volcanic components (Eastwood 1953). The Haweswater dolerite (Fig. 1 and palaeomagnetic sites 5-7 of this study) intrudes the Borrowdale Volcanic Group on either side of Haweswater and was interpreted as a vent related to the group by Nutt (1968). Further to the north theThrelkeld- St John's microgranodiorite (sites 8-14 of this study, Figs 1 and 2) intrudes the base of the Borrowdale Volcanic Group; the study of Wadge et al. For technical reasons this study has been concentrated on the latter (Fig. 3). The lamprophyres are poorly exposed, often highly weathered, grey or brown rocks which show such slight baked margin effects that they must have been intruded at low magmatic temperatures (Burgess and Wadge 1974). They cannot readily be differentiated in the field and their petrologic affinities have only been resolved by thorough analysis of thin sections. Introduction In certain circumstances the palaeomagnetic method can be employed to date episodes of igneous intrusion where reliable age data cannot otherwise be obtained by conventional radiometric methods. It involves isolating primary directions of magnetisation from the rock body, determining the corresponding palaeomagnetic pole, and comparing this pole with the apparent polar wander (a.p.w.) path for the region independently established from studies on dated rocks. The palaeomagnetic method of dating has the advantage that many more rock units can be surveyed than is practicable with the Rb-Sr method, and it does not suffer from the difficulties of interpretation caused by variable argon loss in the K-Ar method. Brown and W. A. Morris This study employs palaeomagnetism to differentiate between Palaeozoic minor intrusionsinnorthern England. The lamprophyres of the Cross Fell Inlier subdivide petrographically into kersantites and minettes. All the kersantites have steep directions of magnetisation probably correlating with an interval of anomalous geomagnetic field in Caradocian times. The Threlkeld-St John’s micro- granodiorite (445 m.y.) and Carrock Fell dolerite dyke swarm also possess steep magnetisations assigned to the same interval. The minettes have shallow directions of magnetisation similar to the Shap Granite (393 m.y.) and correlate with the later Caledonian intrusions of northern England. These episodes of intrusion are separated by late-Silurian tectonism and definea trend of increasing K20/Nar0 in the later magmas of the Caledonian orogeny. Miscellaneous palaeomagnetic results from the Borrowdale Volcanic Group, Embleton diorites and Haweswater dolerite are also reported. 1. For technical reasons this study has been concentrated on the latter (Fig. 3). The lamprophyres are poorly exposed, often highly weathered, grey or brown rocks which show such slight baked margin effects that they must have been intruded at low magmatic temperatures (Burgess and Wadge 1974). They cannot readily be differentiated in the field and their petrologic affinities have only been resolved by thorough analysis of thin sections. Brown and W. A. Morris This study employs palaeomagnetism to differentiate between Palaeozoic minor intrusionsinnorthern England. The lamprophyres of the Cross Fell Inlier subdivide petrographically into kersantites and minettes. All the kersantites have steep directions of magnetisation probably correlating with an interval of anomalous geomagnetic field in Caradocian times. The Threlkeld-St John’s micro- granodiorite (445 m.y.) and Carrock Fell dolerite dyke swarm also possess steep magnetisations assigned to the same interval. The minettes have shallow directions of magnetisation similar to the Shap Granite (393 m.y.) and correlate with the later Caledonian intrusions of northern England. These episodes of intrusion are separated by late-Silurian tectonism and definea trend of increasing K20/Nar0 in the later magmas of the Caledonian orogeny. Miscellaneous palaeomagnetic results from the Borrowdale Volcanic Group, Embleton diorites and Haweswater dolerite are also reported. 1. Introduction In certain circumstances the palaeomagnetic method can be employed to date episodes of igneous in

of the north Lake District comprising basalts and basaltic andesites (Eastwood et al. 1965) commenced during the Didymograptus bifidus time zone of the Llanvirn (Downie and Soper 1972), and was tilted prior to eruption of the Borrowdale Volcanic Group (palaeomagnetic sites 1 to 4 of this study), comprising predominantly andesites and rhyolites (Firman 1957; Mitchell 1956; Moseley 1960, 1964). This latter group lies unconformably on Llanvirnian slates east of Keswick but may be essentially conformable in the southwest of the Lake District outcrop; it was in turn folded and partly eroded prior to deposition of the (Caradocian) Coniston Limestone Group including minor volcanic components (Eastwood 1953). The Haweswater dolerite (Fig. 1 and palaeomagnetic sites 5-7 of this study) intrudes the Borrowdale Volcanic Group on either side of Haweswater and was interpreted as a vent related to the group by Nutt (1968). Introduction In certain circumstances the palaeomagnetic method can be employed to date episodes of igneous intrusion where reliable age data cannot otherwise be obtained by conventional radiometric methods. It involves isolating primary directions of magnetisation from the rock body, determining the corresponding palaeomagnetic pole, and comparing this pole with the apparent polar wander (a.p.w.) path for the region independently established from studies on dated rocks. The palaeomagnetic method of dating has the advantage that many more rock units can be surveyed than is practicable with the Rb-Sr method, and it does not suffer from the difficulties of interpretation caused by variable argon loss in the K-Ar method. However, a success- ful application depends critically on a number of factors. Firstly, the age of the rock unit must be known within broad limits; secondly the

Brown and W. A. Morris This study employs palaeomagnetism to differentiate between Palaeozoic minor intrusionsinnorthern England. The lamprophyres of the Cross Fell Inlier subdivide petrographically into kersantites and minettes. All the kersantites have steep directions of magnetisation probably correlating with an interval of anomalous geomagnetic field in Caradocian times. The Threlkeld-St John’s micro- granodiorite (445 m.y.) and Carrock Fell dolerite dyke swarm also possess steep magnetisations assigned to the same interval. The minettes have shallow directions of magnetisation similar to the Shap Granite (393 m.y.) and correlate with the later Caledonian intrusions of northern England. These episodes of intrusion are separated by late-Silurian tectonism and definea trend of increasing K20/Nar0 in the later magmas of the Caledonian orogeny. Miscellaneous palaeomagnetic results from the Borrowdale Volcanic Group, Embleton diorites and Haweswater dolerite are also reported. 1. Introduction In certain circumstances the palaeomagnetic method can be employed to date episodes of igneous in

of the north Lake District comprising basalts and basaltic andesites (Eastwood et al. 1965) commenced during the Didymograptus bifidus time zone of the Llanvirn (Downie and Soper 1972), and was tilted prior to eruption of the Borrowdale Volcanic Group (palaeomagnetic sites 1 to 4 of this study), comprising predominantly andesites and rhyolites (Firman 1957; Mitchell 1956; Moseley 1960, 1964). This latter group lies unconformably on Llanvirnian slates east of Keswick but may be essentially conformable in the southwest of the Lake District outcrop; it was in turn folded and partly eroded prior to deposition of the (Caradocian) Coniston Limestone Group including minor volcanic components (Eastwood 1953). The Haweswater dolerite (Fig. 1 and palaeomagnetic sites 5-7 of this study) intrudes the Borrowdale Volcanic Group on either side of Haweswater and was interpreted as a vent related to the group by Nutt (1968). (1976) confirms that this body is.Ordovician in age (Rb-Sr isochron, 445f15 m.y.). In the vicinity of Embleton,northwestofBassenthwaite, the Skiddaw Slatesare intruded by asuite of many min

This suggests that intrusion and magnetization of the Moreno Complex and the metamorphism and remagnetization of the Jorgina Formation were related to batholith emplacement. Extracted stable components of magnetization from all units (17 sites) define site-mean directions with a scattered distribution. The scatter in site-mean directions is interpreted as being due to minor, localized, non-uniform, block-fault related (normal or strike-slip, or both) rotation after 158 Ma. cal data from an Early Palaeozoic high grade metamorphic complex (Jorgina Forma- tion) and Jurassic layered basic intrusion (Moreno Complex) are reported from the Mejillones Peninsula of northern Chile (23-23'30's). 40Ar-39Ar dates from the Lower Palaeozoic Jorgina Formation and the Moreno Complex are between 170 and 158 Ma, coincident with a phase of emplacement of the north Chilean coastal batholith. Paleomagnetic data for three Late Paleozoic formations from the Argentine Andes are reported. These formations are: the Majaditas For- mation, exposed at 31.8°S 69.4°W (Precordillera) assigned to the Middle Carboniferous; the Portezuelo del Cenizo Formation, exposed at 32.1°S 69.5°W (Cordillera Frontal) with a radiometric age of 275±10 Ma (Early Permian) and the Choiyoi Formation, exposed at 39.1°S 70.5°W (Cordillera Principal), assigned to the Permo-Triassic. Introduction Several authors have recently suggested the possible existence of alloch- thonous terranes in southwestern South America (Nur and Ben Avraham, 1977,1978; Martinez, 1980; Dalmayrac et al, 1980; Ramos, 1984; Ramos et al, 1984, 1986). Particularly, Vilas and Valencio (1982; see also Valencio and Vilas, 1985) carried out a paleomagnetic study of some late Paleozoic rocks from the Cordillera Frontal, Argentina (Yalguaraz Formation, Upper Carboniferous? and Portezuelo del Cenizo Formation, Early Permian; sampling area 2, Figure 1). The paleomagnetic pole positions obtained for these formations differ considerably from those for age-equivalent rocks from stable zones of South America. These authors interpreted these results in terms of two different hypotheses. One suggested a large "in situ" clock- wise rotation of site 2 around a vertical axis after Permian times. Particularly, Vilas and Valencio (1982; see also Valencio and Vilas, 1985) carried out a paleomagnetic study of some late Paleozoic rocks from the Cordillera Frontal, Argentina (Yalguaraz Formation, Upper Carboniferous? and Portezuelo del Cenizo Formation, Early Permian; sampling area 2, Figure 1). The paleomagnetic pole positions obtained for these formations differ considerably from those for age-equivalent rocks from stable zones of South America. The sedimentary rocks of the Izumi Group occupy a 5-10 km wide basin that extends for approximately 300 km from northwestern Shikoku to Kii Peninsula. Most of the sediments succession consists of a turbidite facies of sandstone and shale interbedded with thin acidic tuff layers. The succession lies unconformably on metamorphic rocks and granite of the Ryoke metamorphic Belt to the north, and contacts the Sanbagawa metamorphic rocks along the MTL to the south. Basal conglomerates and coarse-grained sandstone, rich in rock fragments transported from the Ryoke Belt, are distributed widely along the northern margin of the basin. The Izumi Group contains no detritus from the Sanbagawa Belt [Kanmera and Hashimoto, 1980]. The axial part of the basin is underlain by interbedded sandstone and mudstone, which grade northward into finely bedded and massive layers of mudstone.

A paleomagnetic study was made on the two categories, the material boundary and the Pleistocene strata in the Oiso Hills located along mechanical boundary zone, when one consider in the boundary between the Philippine Sea plate and detail the tectonism on and near the surface of the northeast Japan arc. This study evaluates the subduction zones. The material boundary is a sense and amount of the Quaternary deformation as- sociated with the interaction between the plates. About 170 sedimentary rock samples ranging in age from 0.2 to 1.0 Ma were measured. We used alter - nating field and thermal demagnetization to ex- amine the stability of the natural remanent mag- netizations. The mean field directions from the Numashiro. the Ninomiya, and the Haneo Formations, which range in age from 0.2 to 0.7 Ma, are nearly aligned with the present axial geocentric dipole field. ace of the northeast Japan arc. This study evaluates the subduction zones. The material boundary is a sense and amount of the Quaternary deformation as- sociated with the interaction between the plates. About 170 sedimentary rock samples ranging in age from 0.2 to 1.0 Ma were measured. We used alter - nating field and thermal demagnetization to ex- amine the stability of the natural remanent mag- netizations. The mean field directions from the Numashiro. the Ninomiya, and the Haneo Formations, which range in age from 0.2 to 0.7 Ma, are nearly aligned with the present axial geocentric dipole field. In contrast, the directions from the Maekawa Formation. which ranges in age from 0.8 to 1.0 Ma, show on average 50 clockwise deflections . of declination. These deflections are probably caused by clockwise tectonic rotation between 0.6 and 0.9 Ma. We propose and discuss three models of the rotation mechanism, (1) local drag along a major strike-slip fault, (2) regional dextral shear along the plate boundary, and (3) oroclinal bending caused by collision of a buoyant terrane. A paleomagnetic study was made on the two categories, the material boundary and the Pleistocene strata in the Oiso Hills located along mechanical boundary zone, when one consider in the boundary between the Philippine Sea plate and detail the tectonism on and near the surface of the northeast Japan arc. This study evaluates the subduction zones. The material boundary is a sense and amount of the Quaternary deformation as- sociated with the interaction between the plates. About 170 sedimentary rock samples ranging in age from 0.2 to 1.0 Ma were measured. We used alter - nating field and thermal demagnetization to ex- amine the stability of the natural remanent mag- netizations. The mean field directions from the Numashiro. the Ninomiya, and the Haneo Formations, which range in age from 0.2 to 0.7 Ma, are nearly aligned with the present axial geocentric dipole field. ace of the northeast Japan arc. This study evaluates the subduction zones. The material boundary is a sense and amount of the Quaternary deformation as- sociated with the interaction between the plates. About 170 sedimentary rock samples ranging in age from 0.2 to 1.0 Ma were measured. We used alter - nating field and thermal demagnetization to ex- amine the stability of the natural remanent mag- netizations. The mean field directions from the Numashiro. the Ninomiya, and the Haneo Formations, which range in age from 0.2 to 0.7 Ma, are nearly aligned with the present axial geocentric dipole field. In contrast, the directions from the Maekawa Formation. which ranges in age from 0.8 to 1.0 Ma, show on average 50 clockwise deflections . of declination. These deflections are probably caused by clockwise tectonic rotation between 0.6 and 0.9 Ma. We propose and discuss three models of the rotation mechanism, (1) local drag along a major strike-slip fault, (2) regional dextral shear along the plate boundary, and (3) oroclinal bending caused by collision of a buoyant terrane. There is evidence that some lithologies, mainly fine-grained siltstones carry some characteristic magnetization and some contribution to magnetostrati- graphy can be made. In the Spanish Permo-Triassic rocks studied in this paper there is quite unequivocal evidence that much of the magnetic remanence originated during diagenesis. This is in the form of palaeomagnetic directions which lie near the present geomagnetic field and also diagenetic studies which show abundant authigenic hematite as pore-lining and pore-filling phases. In particular we can position the upper boundary of the Kiaman Epoch with reference to the biostratigraphy and we discuss the origin and significance of both the characteristic and secondary magnetizations. Stratigraphical and sedimentological background At the end of the Hercynian orogeny (Late Carboniferous- Early Permian), the Iberian Peninsula suffered a complex wrench faulting process with two main east-west systems (the northern Pyrenean-Bay of Biscay system and the Gibraltar system). An important NW-SE and NE-SW fault system developed in the interior of the Iberian Plate, forming di

stic remanence which is exclusively reversed and corresponds to the Kiaman Interval of Lower Permian age. A pole position (49N, 167 W) is consistent with previous studies which indicate the rotation of Iberia in post-Triassic times relative to the stable European plate. The Saxonian facies show complex, multicomponent magnetizations; no polarity zonation can be resolved but individual components were acquired prior to the rotation of Iberia. The Buntsandstein is remarkable in that much of it is completely remagnetized in a direction similar to the present local geomagnetic direction. This secondary remanence is carried by fine grained hematite which has been formed as a result of carbonate dissolution and other diagenetic reactions. Initially, these iron oxides were probably superparamagnetic and remanence was only blocked-in by structural inversion of the Iberian Cordillera in Tertiary times and after rotation of the Iberian plate. Some of the primary remanence is preserved in some fine grained lithologies of the Buntsandstein, indicating that normal and reversed zones of magnetization were originally present. The magnetiza- tion of the Muschelkalk carbonates is also complex; secondary components similar to those of the Buntsandstein are present but there is evidence that p

Four stratigraphical units comprising the Autunian, ‘Saxonian’, Buntsandstein and Muschelkalk have been studied in a single section near Molina de Aragon which is well-documented sedimentologically. Autunian rocks have a characteristic remanence which is exclusively reversed and corresponds to the Kiaman Interval of Lower Permian age. A pole position (49N, 167 W) is consistent with previous studies which indicate the rotation of Iberia in post-Triassic times relative to the stable European plate. The Saxonian facies show complex, multicomponent magnetizations; no polarity zonation can be resolved but individual components were acquired prior to the rotation of Iberia. The Buntsandstein is remarkable in that much of it is completely remagnetized in a direction similar to the present local geomagnetic direction. This secondary remanence is carried by fine grained hematite which has been formed as a result of carbonate dissolution and other diagenetic reactions. Initially, these iron oxides were probably superparamagnetic and remanence was only blocked-in by structural inversion of the Iberian Cordillera in Tertiary times and after rotation of the Iberian plate. In this paper our aim is to discuss the origin of the magnetization and determine if secondary (diagenetic) remanence can be isolated to reveal characteristic magnetizations. There is evidence that some lithologies, mainly fine-grained siltstones carry some characteristic magnetization and some contribution to magnetostrati- graphy can be made. In the Spanish Permo-Triassic rocks studied in this paper there is quite unequivocal evidence that much of the magnetic remanence originated during diagenesis. This is in the form of palaeomagnetic directions which lie near the present geomagnetic field and also diagenetic studies which show abundant authigenic hematite as pore-lining and pore-filling phases. In particular we can position the upper boundary of the Kiaman Epoch with reference to the biostratigraphy and we discuss the origin and significance of both the characteristic and secondary magnetizations. carrier_investigation_candidates.excerpt: Scotland. The samples were collected from the Eishort anticline, a large recumbent fold of Caledonian age. The sofrer component (which is demagnetized by low temperatures and weak magnetic fields), when in situ, displays a steep upward direction typical of reversed Tertiary magnetizations. Both polarities of the harder component (which is demagnetized by high temperatures only) are present and, when dip corrected, display either northwesterly upward or southeasterly downward directions characteristic of Torridonian remanences. It is suggested that the Tertiary component is of chemical origin and the result of alteration of magnetite (titanomagnetite) grains. The geographical distribution of these grains is irregular and as a result the distribution of the Tertiary overprint is irregular. The Torridonian palaeomagnetic components from both limbs of the fold can be restored by rotation about the fold axis to internally consistent directions which lie close to previously published data from the Caledonian foreland. No correction is necessary for finite strain which suggests that the Eishort anticline formed by a flexural slip mechanism. However, an anticlockwise rotation of 26" is required to reconcile the Torridonian directions from the Kishorn nappe with those of the Caledonian for

Discussion and conclusions Two geologically significant palaeomagnetic components can be identified in the samples of Torridonian sandstones collected from the Eishort anticline of Skye. The softer component is of Tertiary age (Table 2, Fig. 7b and d). This age is indicated by a negative fold test (Graham 1949; McElhinny 1964) and close similarity to previously published palaeomagnetic data from Tertiary igneous rocks. This component is only present in those specimens which contain suitable grains (those of categories B and C). The remagnetization is obviously a consequence of the Tertiary igneous activity but the laboratory blocking temperatures indicate regional temperatures far in excess of those which might reasonably be expected for the area. Therefore, the Tertiary remanence must be of chemical origin and is present only in those specimens which contained grains capable of being modified or altered. Furthermore, it is

wart 1969). Since the original work of Irving & Runcorn (1957) these rocks have been the subject of several palaeomagnetic investigations. Irving & Runcorn (1957) established the presence of stable magnetizations of Torridonian age and were able to demonstrate a marked difference in palaeomagnetic direction between the upper and lower parts of the sequence. Subsequent geological work (Stewart 1966) showed the presence of an unconfor- mity between what later became defined as the Stoer and Torridon Groups. All Torridonian stratigraphical names used in this paper conform to those of Stewart (1%9). Using thermal and alternating field demagnetization techniques Stewart & Irving (1974) were able to confirm and refine the work of Irving & Runcorn (1957) and show that the change in remanent direction is associated with the unconformity. McClelland (1976), using alternating field techniques, studied the magneto-stratigraphy of the Applecross Formation and recognized a reversal stratigraphy com- patible with the previous studies. Recently the magneto- stratigraphy of the Applecross and Aultbea Formations has been investigated by Smith et al. (1983). Given the different ranges of detrital grain sizes described above it is possible that these differences are of sedimentary origin and were established at deposition. Discussion and conclusions Two geologically significant palaeomagnetic components can be identified in the samples of Torridonian sandstones collected from the Eishort anticline of Skye. The softer component is of Tertiary age (Table 2, Fig. 7b and d). This age is indicated by a negative fold test (Graham 1949; McElhinny 1964) and close similarity to previously published palaeomagnetic data from Tertiary igneous rocks. This component is only present in those specimens which contain suitable grains (those of categories B and C). The remagnetization is obviously a consequence of the Tertiary igneous activity but the laboratory blocking temperatures indicate regional temperatures far in excess of those which might reasonably be expected for the area. Therefore, the Tertiary remanence must be of chemical origin and is present only in those specimens which contained grains capable of being modified or altered. Furthermore, it is

Furthermore, it is suggested that the geographical and stratigraphical distribu- tion of these grains was imposed during deposition in late Precambrian times. The harder component is of Torridonian age (Table 1, Fig. 7a and c) and is present in specimens of categories A and C. Irving & Runcorn (1957) established the presence of stable magnetizations of Torridonian age and were able to demonstrate a marked difference in palaeomagnetic direction between the upper and lower parts of the sequence. Subsequent geological work (Stewart 1966) showed the presence of an unconfor- mity between what later became defined as the Stoer and Torridon Groups. Additional information is available as a Supplementary Publica­ tion (SUP 24015). GEOLOGY AND AGE The Torridonian sediments are a thick, largely undeformed, suite of clastic sediments of predominantly fluviatile origin (Peach et al. 1907; Selley and Stewart 1967) lying unconformably on a degraded erosion surface of Lewisian gneiss. They include a major angular unconformity of 25-30° (Lawson 1965; Williams 1966; Stewart 1966) separating the Upper Torridonian from the Stoer Group (Stewart 19.69), and are overlain by quartzites of Lower Cambrian age which dip at angles of up to 30° towards the Moine Thrust Zone of the Caledonian orogenic belt (c. 500-400 Ma) in the east. Final stages in the uplift of the older Lewisian complex are represented by K-Ar ages on biotites from Torridon of 1094 ± 42 Ma (Miller and Brown 1965), 1114 ± 30 Ma (Moorbath et al. 1967) and 1148 and 1169 Ma (Moorbath and Park 1972), and by a K-Ar whole-rock age from the Gairloch district of 1094 ± 45 Ma (Evans and Park 1965). GEOLOGY AND AGE The Torridonian sediments are a thick, largely undeformed, suite of clastic sediments of predominantly fluviatile origin (Peach et al. 1907; Selley and Stewart 1967) lying unconformably on a degraded erosion surface of Lewisian gneiss. They include a major angular unconformity of 25-30° (Lawson 1965; Williams 1966; Stewart 1966) separating the Upper Torridonian from the Stoer Group (Stewart 19.69), and are overlain by quartzites of Lower Cambrian age which dip at angles of up to 30° towards the Moine Thrust Zone of the Caledonian orogenic belt (c. 500-400 Ma) in the east. Final stages in the uplift of the older Lewisian complex are represented by K-Ar ages on biotites from Torridon of 1094 ± 42 Ma (Miller and Brown 1965), 1114 ± 30 Ma (Moorbath et al. 1967) and 1148 and 1169 Ma (Moorbath and Park 1972), and by a K-Ar whole-rock age from the Gairloch district of 1094 ± 45 Ma (Evans and Park 1965).
