SAMPLING Each palaeomagnetic site comprises an average of six separate cores drilled from the same bedded unit and oriented prior to extraction by sun sights and/or magnetic bearings. In stratigraphic sections the sampled sites are separated by thicknesses of between 5 and 50 m (Fig. 1); stratigraphic columns are derived from altitude determinations in conjunction with dip

ation (SUP 24015). Frequently the cleaning treatment increases within-site dispersion but is a necessary complement to the study because it at Purdue University Library on July 20, 2015http://sjg.lyellcollection.org/Downloaded from PALAEOMAGNETISM OF THE TORRIDONIAN 35 removes a secondary component and results in systematic movement of the remanence vectors (Fig. 3); this is believed to reflect the grain size effect observed by Irving (1957) where the internal dispersion increases with grain size which controls the degree of alignment with the palaeofield direction. Slump horizons in the Aultbea Formation yield random directions and fold tests yield an improve­ ment in overall precisions but structural dips are not large enough to yield definitive tests. Chemical leaching experiments have successfully removed all of the red ochre pigment but show no significant reduction in the magnitude or direction of remanences in most samples, confirming that the bulk of this resides in the specularite grains; the exceptions are a few Applecross and Aultbea samples showing minor clockwise rotation of the vector similar to the results of thermal treatment. Analysis of the minor secondary component of magnetization present in the Torridonian sediments is also described in the supplement

The Ballantrae complex is an obducted ophiolite relict of this ocean (Dewey 1969), S of which a trench was infilled with turbidites and flysch-facies sediments in Ordovician and Silurian times. The relative position of this region is critical to models linking the destruction of the basin to stages in the development of the orthotectonic Caledonides to the N and the paratectonic Caledonides to the S. The documented models include an oceanic plate thrust northwards under the orthotec­ tonic Caledonides (Dewey and Pankhurst 1970), a plate thrust southwards under the broad area of the paratectonic Caledonides (Fitton and Hughes 1970), paired sub- duction zones beneath the Highland Boundary Fault and Southern Uplands Fault with the Midland Valley as a relict of the Iapetus Ocean (Gunn 1973), northwesterly subduction beneath the Southern Uplands (Mitchell and McKerrow 1975), and convergence between the Southern Uplands region and Northern England along a triple junction migrating progressively to the SW (Phillips et al. 1976). GEOLOGICAL OUTLINE The Ballantrae Complex has formed the subject of a long history of geological study, and following the classical work of Nicol, Murchison, Lapworth, Peach and Home, interest has continued in the present century with the structural and petrologic studies of Balsillie (1932), Anderson (1936) Bailey and McCallien (1957) and Williams (1962). During the past decade interest in the complex has centred on its ophiolitic affinities and, as the largest exposed body of its kind in the British Caledonides, is critical to the models listed above. The rocks available for study are hardly suitable for a complete resolution of this problem because the Middle Arenig pillow lavas inter­ preted as ancient Iapetus crust (Dewey 1971) were highly deformed and subjected to high pressure, low temperature metamorphism. Deformation was accompanied by widespread development of serpentinite and intrusion of gabbro; these rocks provide opportunity to study later events. Sampling for this

Post-Arenig, pre-Caradocian gabbros and serpentinites of the Ballantrae Complex yield palaeomagnetic poles of 26°E, 10°S (dy = 10-9, d* = 18-8°) and 27°E, 12°S (dy = 5.5, dx = 9-7°) respectively after a.f. and thermal cleaning. Although 95 per cent confidence circles overlap with other British Ordovician data, magnetic inclinations are systematically shallower than contemporaneous results from England and Wales and correlate closely with other data from N of the Southern Uplands Fault line. A similar result is found from palaeomagnetic study of the (Lower Caradocian) Bail Hill Volcanics. The palaeomagnetic results support faunal and tectonic evidence that the major crustal separation in Ordovician times existed between the Southern Uplands and the northern Lake District. The visible ophiolite slices along the approximate line of the present Midland Valley represent pre- Llanvirnian obduction in a northerly direction of an earlier ocean basin. INTRODUCTION The Caledonian orogenic cycle was associated with the development and con­ sumption of the Iapetus (Proto-Atlantic) ocean basin (Wilson 1966, Harland and Gayer 1972). (1973, fig. 3) find that Lower Ordovician rock units from the British Isles have systematically shallower palaeomagnetic inclinations in regions N of the Highland Boundary Fault compared with regions S of the fault. Better consistency with the geomagnetic axial dipole model is achieved if a crustal separation of about 1000 km is postulated between the Highland Boundary Fault and the Northern Lake District. Unfor­ tunately, because of the statistical nature of palaeomagnetic results this estimate has a large associated uncertainty (±800 km), and it is only because all results from S of the postulated suture have steeper palaeomagnetic inclinations to all results from N of the suture that the observation can be viewed with some confidence. Development of the Southern Uplands Block thus took place within a narrow ocean basin, and defining its position within this basin by palaeomagnetic study is further hampered by the paucity of relatively undeformed igneous rocks. The Ballantrae complex is an obducted ophiolite relict of this ocean (Dewey 1969), S of which a trench was infilled with turbidites and flysch-facies sediments in Ordovician and Silurian times. The relative position of this region is critical to models linking the destruction of the basin to stages in the development of the orthotectonic Caledonides to the N and the paratectonic Caledonides to the S. The documented models include an oceanic plate thrust northwards under the orthotec­ tonic Caledonides (Dewey and Pankhurst 1970), a plate thrust southwards under the broad area of the paratectonic Caledonides (Fitton and Hughes 1970), paired sub- duction zones beneath the Highland Boundary Fault and Southern Uplands Fault with the Midland Valley as a relict of the Iapetus Ocean (Gunn 1973), northwesterly subduction beneath the Southern Uplands (Mitchell and McKerrow 1975), and convergence between the Southern Uplands region and Northern England along a triple junction migrating progressively to the SW (Phillips et al. 1976). PALAEOMAGNETIC RESULTS Cores drilled in the field with a motorized portable drill were oriented by sun and/or magnetic sights and cut into 2-5 cm cylinders for palaeomagnetic meas­ urements with a parastatic magnetometer. All samples were progressively demag­ netized using an alternating field system in steps of 50 or 100 Oersteds (oe.) and remeasured after each step. The stability of magnetic vectors isolated by a.f cleaning was tested by thermally-demagnetizing pilot samples in steps of 100°C to 500°C, then at 530°C and 560°C. Sections from the base of some cores were further utilized for polished section study, and thermomagnetic determinations (saturation mag­ netization, Js, versus temperature) were made on small fragments using a Chevallier balance. The orientation of the susceptibility ellipsoid is described by K max , K int and K min , which are the principal axes of susceptibility. DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSIONS On the origin of remanence and fabric The NRM of the Stoer and Torridon Group sediments (and boulders) can generally be accounted for in terms of a two component magnetization structure. LT components are typically randomized between 400 and 600°C, and HT components carry more than 70 percent of the total NRM. The pattern of discrete unblocking above 600°C indicates that specular haematite is the principal reman­ ence carrier. HT components from the Stoer and Torridon Group are significantly different (in overall agreement with previous studies), and results from the conglomerate test imply that the principal magnetization of the Stoer Group pre-dates the Torridon Group magnetization. Furthermore, comparison of in situ and unfolded HT inclination data from the Stoer boulders indicates that the boulders are likely to have retained a "primary" magnetization, compatible with the Stoer Group magnetization. Bedding orientated magnetic foliation planes and low anisotropy parameters observed from the Stoer and Torridon Group are "typical" of undeformed sediments. Radiometric ages (Rb/Sr, whole rock) of 968 and 777 Ma from the Stoer (siltstone) and Torridon (siltstone-shale) Group respectively, are thought to reflect the timing of diagenesis (isotopic homogenization of Sr). Prior to deposition of Cambro-Ordovician marine deposits, the two groups were weakly folded, uplifted and eroded. This account deals with palaeomagnetic properties of the Torridonian sedi­ ments with particular emphasis on the origin and stability of remanence, and of the magnetic fabric. The Stoer Group, which comprises some 2 km of clastic sediments, was sampled from 15 sites covering the Stoer and Achiltibuie regions (Fig. 1). Palaeocurrent reversals in lake deposits suggest a rift controlled origin with active marginal faults (Stewart 1983). A similar origin has also been suggested for the younger Torridon Group, which embraces c. 7 km of essentially continental elastics divided into four formations (the Diabaig, Applecross, Aultbea and Cailleach Formations). DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSIONS On the origin of remanence and fabric The NRM of the Stoer and Torridon Group sediments (and boulders) can generally be accounted for in terms of a two component magnetization structure. LT components are typically randomized between 400 and 600°C, and HT components carry more than 70 percent of the total NRM. The pattern of discrete unblocking above 600°C indicates that specular haematite is the principal reman­ ence carrier. HT components from the Stoer and Torridon Group are significantly different (in overall agreement with previous studies), and results from the conglomerate test imply that the principal magnetization of the Stoer Group pre-dates the Torridon Group magnetization. Furthermore, comparison of in situ and unfolded HT inclination data from the Stoer boulders indicates that the boulders are likely to have retained a "primary" magnetization, compatible with the Stoer Group magnetization. Bedding orientated magnetic foliation planes and low anisotropy parameters observed from the Stoer and Torridon Group are "typical" of undeformed sediments. n a low-field susceptibility bridge (KLY-1) for a total of 11 sites. The magnetic susceptibility is a symmetric, second order tensor expressed as a triaxial ellipsoid. The orientation of the susceptibility ellipsoid is described by K max , K int and K min , which are the principal axes of susceptibility. The axial ratios PI (Lineation: K max /K int ), P2 (Anisotropy: Km^/Ka^n), P3 (Foliation: K^/l"^^) and E (Eccentricity: P1/P2) are used to describe the shape of the magnetic ellipsoids. The magnetic fabric in undeformed sediments may comprise two elements: 1) a magnetic foliation essentially in the bedding plane due to gravitational forces (and post-depositional compaction), and 2) lineation or preferred grain orientation (either shape or magnetocrystalline origin) depending on the hydrodynamic environment or the influence of the external field (Rees and Woodall 1975). The Stoer Group sediments and the Stoer boulders are characterized essentially by oblate magnetic ellipsoids (apart from one site in the Stoer area) associated with 4 to 9 percent degree of anisotropy. Radiometric ages (Rb/Sr, whole rock) of 968 and 777 Ma from the Stoer (siltstone) and Torridon (siltstone-shale) Group respectively, are thought to reflect the timing of diagenesis (isotopic homogenization of Sr). Prior to deposition of Cambro-Ordovician marine deposits, the two groups were weakly folded, uplifted and eroded. This account deals with palaeomagnetic properties of the Torridonian sedi­ ments with particular emphasis on the origin and stability of remanence, and of the magnetic fabric. The Stoer Group, which comprises some 2 km of clastic sediments, was sampled from 15 sites covering the Stoer and Achiltibuie regions (Fig. 1). Palaeocurrent reversals in lake deposits suggest a rift controlled origin with active marginal faults (Stewart 1983). A similar origin has also been suggested for the younger Torridon Group, which embraces c. 7 km of essentially continental elastics divided into four formations (the Diabaig, Applecross, Aultbea and Cailleach Formations). DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSIONS On the origin of remanence and fabric The NRM of the Stoer and Torridon Group sediments (and boulders) can generally be accounted for in terms of a two component magnetization structure. Radiometric ages (Rb/Sr, whole rock) of 968 and 777 Ma from the Stoer (siltstone) and Torridon (siltstone-shale) Group respectively, are thought to reflect the timing of diagenesis (isotopic homogenization of Sr). Prior to deposition of Cambro-Ordovician marine deposits, the two groups were weakly folded, uplifted and eroded. This account deals with palaeomagnetic properties of the Torridonian sedi­ ments with particular emphasis on the origin and stability of remanence, and of the magnetic fabric. The Stoer Group, which comprises some 2 km of clastic sediments, was sampled from 15 sites covering the Stoer and Achiltibuie regions (Fig. 1). Palaeocurrent reversals in lake deposits suggest a rift controlled origin with active marginal faults (Stewart 1983). A similar origin has also been suggested for the younger Torridon Group, which embraces c. 7 km of essentially continental elastics divided into four formations (the Diabaig, Applecross, Aultbea and Cailleach Formations). The red sandstones have not yet yielded fossils (Francis 1962), but are overlain by the Cementstone Group of the Calciferous Sandstone Measures of Lower Carboniferous age. In the area of the Belhaven shoreline (56-0°N 2-5°W) the Cementstone Group comprises a series of rhythmic alternations of sandstones and mudstones dipping at shallow angles (0 — 10°) to the SE. INTRODUCTION—GEOLOGY AND SAMPLING Sedimentary rocks of Upper Old Red Sandstone and Lower Carboniferous age have been penetrated by volcanic necks and related intrusions in the Dunbar region. The red sandstones have not yet yielded fossils (Francis 1962), but are overlain by the Cementstone Group of the Calciferous Sandstone Measures of Lower Carboniferous age. In the area of the Belhaven shoreline (56-0°N 2-5°W) the Cementstone Group comprises a series of rhythmic alternations of sandstones and mudstones dipping at shallow angles (0 — 10°) to the SE. These have been cut by volcanic tuffs and breccias and then intruded by quartz-dolerite dykes aligned approximately ENE. The widest of these is some 20 m wide (the "Big Dyke"), while a narrower one, c. 0-4 m wide (the "Small" Dyke), lies immediately south and at an angle of c. 20° to the Big Dyke (Fig. 1). The Big Dyke appears fresh, but the Small Dyke comprises haematite-impregnated, argillised (partially converted to clays), carbonated basaltic rock, with closer affinities to the olivine basalt suite rather than to quartz dolerites (A. INTERPRETATION OF THE PALAEOMAGNETIC DATA The mean ChRM directions derived from both non- recrystallized limestones of the Maubisse Formation and from sediments of the Aituto Formation have negative, upward directed inclinations. This implies that if the ChRM is depositional or early post-depositional, and was acquired in an area located in the magnetic southern hemisphere, the sediments were magnetized during a period of normal magnetic polarity. We shall demonstrate that the studied sediments may have a southern origin. INTERPRETATION OF THE PALAEOMAGNETIC DATA The mean ChRM directions derived from both non- recrystallized limestones of the Maubisse Formation and from sediments of the Aituto Formation have negative, upward directed inclinations. This implies that if the ChRM is depositional or early post-depositional, and was acquired in an area located in the magnetic southern hemisphere, the sediments were magnetized during a period of normal magnetic polarity. We shall demonstrate that the studied sediments may have a southern origin. The age of the Maubisse Formation is Late Permian-Early Triassic, possibly younger than the Kiaman Interval, a period of reversed magnetic polarity that lasted from the Late Carboniferous through the end of the Permian. During the Triassic time interval a large number of reversals of the earth's magnetic field occurred. The polar swathe correlates with (i) a higher blocking temperature component from the BGR, (ii) the uplift magnetization record in the western orthotectonic Caledonides of Scotland, and (iii) primary magnetizations from the Siluro-Devonian molasse facies in Britain. An investigation in the western sector of the Northern Highlands of Scotland (Watts 1982) illustrates a particular problem associated with metamorphic studies: a comprehensive magnetic imprint of Upper Silurian-Lower Devonian age appears to have gone entirely unrecorded in the K-Ar isotopic record; the metamorphic minerals record argon closure ages which are 10-60Ma older (Dewey & Pankhurst 1970) than the age of magnetic blocking. The remanence also post-dates isother- mal surfaces deformed by the local F3 episode of deformation. In contrast, the Barrovian zones of the Grampian Highlands (Watts 1985) define a remanence acquired between the regional F3 and F4 folding episodes. 2 OUTLINE GEOLOGY The northeastward continuation of the Caledonian orogen into Scandinavia is composed predominantly of a thick nappe pile which was metamorphosed during and after emplacement following closure of the Iapetus suture. Examples from metamorphic material in the lower grades of metamorphism show asymptotic decrease in saturation remanence (I,) with increasing temperature [sample 79 in Fig. 5(b)] linked to a predominance of paramagnetic carriers obeying the Curie Law. Other (usually stable) samples show a discrete magnetite Curie point [samples 3, 35 and 41 in Fig. 5(b) and (c)]. Separation of heating and cooling curves is indicative of magnetic carriers in a metastable condition and alteration during heating in air. Such samples cannot generally be effectively treated by thermal demagnetization. Discrete haematite Curie points [sample 41, Fig. 5(b)] are identified at only a few sites in the BGR but are prominent within the higher grade rocks of the Jotun Nappe, notably in the northern sector of the Jotunheimen granulite massif. etastable condition and alteration during heating in air. Such samples cannot generally be effectively treated by thermal demagnetization. Discrete haematite Curie points [sample 41, Fig. 5(b)] are identified at only a few sites in the BGR but are prominent within the higher grade rocks of the Jotun Nappe, notably in the northern sector of the Jotunheimen granulite massif. Isothermal Remanent Magnetization (IRM) acquisition studies also identify a preponderance of magnetite and/or sulphide carriers in the bulk of this collection, which mostly saturate in fields below 0.5 T (Fig. 6, samples 6, 10, 20 and 39); a smaller fraction of (haematite-bearing) samples continue to show a small progressive increase in IRM above this (Fig. 6, sample 41).
